# The Nordland Coast

*Pages PDF 18-28*

## The Nordland Coast
## **Once a Neglected Backwater, Now the Empire’s Brave New Endeavour**
The Empire’s northern frontier is its shoreline, from the Wasteland to the border with Kislev. The Nordland coast is a bastion against raids from the north, where the maritime legacy of the Empire is found in the bays, coves, and clifftops lashed by the Sea of Claws. 

The Nordland coast is a cold, desolate place, marked by long stretches of isolated dunes and sheer cliffs crumbling into the sea. Human settlements cling to the sloping shore, their lanterns flickering across the waves to ships sailing through the fogs and gloom of the night. Between Wrecker’s Point and the River Demst, the coastline is under the scrutiny of the Eonir, whose woodland realm of Laurelorn covers the western extent of Nordland. Elven and other traders occasionally sail south on the River Demst or Schaukeln deep into the Wood Elf realm. 

After the secession of the Wasteland, the Empire had no major naval or trade port on the coast. Altdorf relies on the Reik for passage to the sea, where Marienburg can exact its tithes for merchants and naval vessels. Nordland has become increasingly important, and after several unsuccessful attempts to build ports to rival Marienburg, there are renewed efforts to assert the Empire’s dominance over the seas. 

In the far west is Wrecker’s Point, a large promontory isolated from the rest of the province and almost lawless. Other than the hard-bitten Nordlanders eking out a living, the headland harbours a tribe of sea-going goblins known as the Reavaz. Further east is the vast sweep of Eiger Bay, with low dunes and windswept shoreline from Hargendorf to Dietershafen. 

The Klauhugel Peninsula is an elevated headland, bisected by the River Salz which flows from Salzenmund to Neues Emskrank. Close to the border with Ostland is Drosselspule Bay, a weed-choked gulf encompassing the monastic isle of Manannsheim. Along the coast are small fishing villages and hamlets, dependent on the Sea of Claws for their livelihood. Smugglers ply their trade in secluded coves and land contraband on moonlit nights. They are ruled by the ‘Smuggler Queen’, a crime lord based in Hargendorf. 

Coastal Nordlanders have weathered millennia of raids from the Norse, Dark Elves, and pirates. There are substantial coastal defences, from sea forts and beacons to fortified islands. 

## **The Imperial Navy**
The Second Fleet had its origins in several Nordland navies owned by the Köhlers, Hargenfels, and Gaussers before 2512 IC. After the Turmoil and petitioning by the Nordland nobility, Karl-Franz agreed to create a new modern fleet to deal with seaborne raiders whose depredations had increased in recent decades. 

The Empire is not a great maritime power. The Asur dominate the world’s oceans, the Bretonnians are better sailors, and the Norse, Tileans, and Estalians greater explorers. Marienburg’s secession has taken the wind from the Empire’s sails. Nonetheless, the Imperial Navy is powerful and many counts and barons want to use it to extend their influence around the globe. 

There is a third Sea Lord, unknown to most of the Navy. Duke Leopold von Bildhofen is building a Third Fleet without the blessing of the Emperor. After his loss of status in the Turmoil, he plans to increase his powerbase and reassert his family’s authority. Carroburg has its own deepwater wharves and might yet serve as a naval port. 

## **The Imperial Sea Lords and the Fleets**
The office of Sea Lord belongs to the most senior admirals in the Imperial Navy, those nobles appointed by the Emperor to oversee the fleets. Officially they administer the Navy, make decisions on governance, administration, and disposition of the fleets. In practice they do as little or much as their ambition dictates. There are officially two Sea Lords, one for each of the Imperial Navy’s fleets. 

## **Imperial Ships**
Most of the First Fleet are Wargalleys, suited to shallow waters. The Second Fleet has a greater proportion of Wolfships, which are being built at a dizzying pace in shipyards along the Nordland coast. Both have their complement of Greatships. There are also experimental vessels — the Ironfist which is armed with a colossal mortar, and the improbable Hellhammer, mounted with a cannon so big it can only carry a handful of cannonballs into battle. Ships are organised into flotillas, made up of squadrons of three ships-of-the-line — the Wargalleys and Wolfships. A Greatship commands each flotilla, with the admiral’s flagship vessel taking overall control. 

The position of Sea Lord of the First Fleet was instituted by Magnus the Pious. It is currently occupied by elderly Lord Adalmann von Hopfberg, who is insane and resides in the Great Hospice. He oversees the Reikland Fleet and has a seat on the Council of State. Practically, the Admiralty (a body of 12 admirals) command the fleet from Altdorf. The boats are dilapidated and the admirals are snobbish and political, vying for position. A recent appointment is Lieutenant Lord Tyrkel von Hargenfels of the Nordland coastal nobility — he resents the patronising treatment he receives from the admirals. There is some confusion about Sea Lord Adalmann von Hopfberg. A man dwelling in his residence in Altdorf claims to be the Sea Lord, even issuing orders at Admiralty House. He has met with admirals and promoted discord, encouraging their ambitions and playing favourites. The First Fleet’s hierarchy are confused, believing von Hopfberg to be sporadically free to leave the hospice. In truth, they are being manipulated by a Grey Wizard, hired by Marienburg to undermine the Admiralty. 

The second Sea Lord is Baron Ludolf Köhler the Younger of Dietershafen. He is young, ambitious, and ‘hands on’. He treats his admirals as peers, delegates responsibility, and is disciplined in the administration of the Second Fleet. The Admiral’s Palace in Dietershafen is a hive of activity, as officers busy themselves following the instructions of the Nordland Naval Chamber and Sea Lord Köhler, issuing orders for new vessels, commissioning officers, and provisioning the growing Second Fleet. 

_Heraldic Crest of the Imperial Sea Lords, depicting Triton wearing fanciful wargear of archaic Imperial design._ 

## **History**
In the first thousand years of the Empire’s existence, the coast was plagued by raids from the seagoing Norse. In response to the sacking of Marienburg in 632 IC, Emperor Hasso decreed that ships and fortifications be built to defend the coast, under the auspices of a new office, the Keepers of the Coast. These nobles raised the first standing navy which fought so hard it forced the Bjornlings, Skaelings, and Sarls to sign treaties at the Althing of Traktatsey in 765 IC. 

However, the navy soon declined. Indifferent nobles let it fall into neglect and by 1300 IC the Norse were once again landing on the Empire’s shores, as settlers and marauders. As the land plunged into civil war, Westerland, Nordland, Ostland, Reikland, and Middenland managed their ageing war fleets as best they could. 

The Westerland Navy forged ahead while the Empire was in disarray. Influenced by Tilean traders visiting Marienburg, they adopted the maritime inventions of the southern nations and soon came to dominate the other provinces in naval power. By the time Magnus the Pious came to power, the only true Empire navy belonged to Westerland, which had ventured beyond the Great Ocean. The uniting Emperor renamed the ramshackle Reikland Navy as the First Fleet and designated Marienburg’s far superior force the Second Fleet. 

This arrangement ended abruptly with Marienburg’s independence. The Empire’s sea power was reduced to the creaking First Fleet (really just a river navy) and a handful of small private navies in Nordland, Ostland, and Middenland. It has taken the ascension of Karl-Franz and the events of the Turmoil to institute a serious naval programme in the Empire and renew interest in overseas exploration and conquest. 

## **The Navy on the Nordland Coast**
The Second Fleet’s home port is Dietershafen. A more secretive base is being established at Norden, away from the watchful eyes of rival powers. The Fleet put in at most significant ports along the Nordland coast, and harbourmasters are expected to make provision for their vessels. There are also numerous seaforts along the Nordland coast owned by the Navy and the coastal Nordland nobility. These include: 

**Fort Odner** — on a barren island in Eiger Bay, Fort Odner stands sentinel over the sea lane west of Dietershafen. It is a miserable posting for the garrison stationed there. 

**Nordenwatch** — a fortified island many miles north of the coast between Nordland and Ostland. The northernmost holding of the Empire. 

**Andel Tower** — an isolated seafort rising from the sea floor, a mile north-east of Dietershafen. An ancient tower, the lowest stairwell descends into long-abandoned flooded chambers. 

There is a series of coastal beacons to warn of invasion or raiders. In theory they link Salzenmund and the whole shoreline in an unbroken chain, each visible from its neighbours when lit. This chain is not without its  ‘weak links.’ Some villagers are derelict in their duty, and  corrupt roadwardens take bribes to leave their beacons unlit. 

## **Traditions**
The Imperial Navy has many traditions and practices. Some are practical, some are superstitious, and many are a mixture of both. 

## **Watchkeeping**
On naval vessels, the day is divided into seven watches timed by hourglass and marked by the ringing of the ship’s bell. During each watch, most of the crew go about their business, while some rest in their cabins. An odd number of watches ensures each crewmember stands a different watch on successive days: 

## **Ship’s Watches**
|Middle Watch|Midnight–4 am|
|---|---|
|Morning Watch (often<br>called Manann’s Watch)|4 am–8 am|
|Forenoon Watch|8 am–Noon|
|Afternoon Watch|Noon–4 pm|
|First Dog Watch|4 pm–6 pm|
|Second Dog Watch|6 pm–8 pm|
|First Watch (often called<br>Beloved Watch,<br>referring to Mannslieb)|8pm–Midnight|

## **’ the Ship S Bell**
The bell does more than mark time. On naval vessels it rings to mark the arrival of an officer on board or to commemorate a death at sea. Services and prayers to Manann are punctuated by pealing the bell and, on a more prosaic level, it is used during fog to alert other vessels of the ship’s presence. 

Veteran seamen can distinguish between seemingly identical bells’ tolls, claiming each has its own personality. When a naval ship goes down, they believe its bell can be heard ringing the watches from the sea floor. 

## **Flags and Pennants**
The Imperial Navy has developed a system of flag codes to communicate with other vessels, both friend and foe. Ensigns are heraldic flags flown to denote the station of the vessel within the Navy, its home province, squadron, and whether a senior officer is on board. If the ensign is flown upside-down, this denotes there is sickness on board and other vessels should stay distant. 

Pennants are used to exchange messages between vessels in a squadron or flotilla. These square flags represent letters, numbers, and common orders. They are usually strung in sequence on the foremast stays. Sending or reading a signal does not require special skills, just access to a Naval Almanack with a key to each pennant’s meaning. 

## **Captain’s Whistle**
Whistles are used by ships’ captains to command their crew on land and at sea. When a new officer is commissioned to the Second Fleet, he is given a ceremonial gold whistle by Grand Baron Gausser. First Fleet officers are expected to inherit their whistles and (all too often) their rank in the Navy. 

## **Baron Ludolf Köhler the Younger**
**Motivation:** Prove to his father that he is more than capable in command. 

**Short-Term Ambition:** Build a powerful, innovative fleet to make Nordland proud. 

**Long-Term Ambition:** Extend the Empire’s reach and power at sea, through exploration and naval might. 

Ludolf Köhler has recently taken the coveted position of Imperial Sea Lord, the first commander of the Second Fleet since Marienburg betrayed the Empire. He is enthusiastic and proud to take up a title his family have long coveted, especially his father — Baron Ludolf the Elder has politicked tirelessly to see the Emperor’s Navy established in Nordland. 

Those who meet Baron Ludolf the Younger are struck by his vigour and restlessness. Decades of sea winds and harsh sunlight have aged him beyond his 32 years, yet he has the energy and appetite for innovation of a man yet to prove himself. Ludolf bounces ideas around, asks people’s opinions, and throws himself into every task at hand. His supporters enjoy his company and lack of airs. His detractors sneer that he’s trying too hard to impress his father — the real power behind the Second Fleet. 

Ludolf the Younger knows all too well his father sees him as merely a cipher. It is starting to rankle, especially when his ideas are ignored or discounted as unworkable. Both Ludolfs are trying to build a modern fleet, but the Younger seeks new invention while the Elder trusts in proven ship-building. The Sea Lord is spending more and more time at Schloss Neurath in Norden, fascinated by the inventions in progress. He is also looking to recruit Celestial, Jade, and Grey Magisters for the fleet. His brother Xavier is an Astromancer and the two conspire with one another to bring more wizardry to the Navy. 

The Nordland Fleet’s admirals are a mixture of old sea dogs and young peers of Ludolf. There are several Köhler cousins — the Admiralty is a family concern and other naval dynasties, such as the von Hargenfels, have been shut out. Relations between Ludolf the Younger and his admirals are good. He prefers not to pull rank and values the experience of older sailors in his command, often accompanying them to hunt pirates. Ludolf is a patron of the Nordland Seahawks regiment, but he worries about how Captain Dreist looks at his wife. 

## **Ludolf the Younger as a Patron**
The Sea Lord has day-to-day responsibilities to the Second Fleet and an overbearing father dictating his decisions. This makes it difficult for him to pursue some of his more adventurous ambitions, so a group of resourceful Characters would be very helpful to him — especially if they’re discreet. 

In exchange for service, the powerful Sea Lord can support a party who want to travel by sea. He can also provide positions in the Navy, or introductions to members of Nordland’s nobility and Altdorf ’s top-ranking military. 

## Find the Lady
Lady Helene Köhler is an explorer, currently in Lustria. She is also the Sea Lord’s younger sister. Ludolf believes the new deep harbour at Norden will help the Empire establish permanent colonies in the New World and therefore acquire a near-limitless supply of gold. The last he heard, his sister was in Port Reaver. He wants to find where she is and extend Köhler influence across the ocean.

## Landship Ahoy!
Baron Köhler is fascinated by the Marienburg landships. He wants to build a flotilla of them for the Second Fleet. Why should the limits of the ocean dictate where the Navy can go? He would like the party to steal one… or at least take the plans from Marsh Warden Ambrosius’s office in Marienburg. 

## **Dietershafen**
Dietershafen has always harboured warships and fishing fleets. Now it’s boomed to become the most important seaport on the Empire’s coast. Where once there were disorganised frigates, there is now a well-drilled fleet, overseen by the Imperial Sea Lord from the Admiral’s Palace. Imperial luminaries visit the docks to inspect the ships, the taverns are full of naval companies, and maritime trades on the waterfront are thriving. 

The town is located in a natural harbour which has been extended along the shore to accommodate fortifications, shipyards, and docks. The original site of the town is known as the ‘Old City’, where fish and vegetable peddlers, simple traders, and the poorest of locals make their home. 

The people here are proud of Dietershafen and even the most destitute holds a naive belief that the Emperor and Baron Ludolf the Elder have their best interests at heart. 

The New City encompasses the main harbour and fortified naval docks, shipyards, and warehouses, along with the residences of townsfolk who work in trades related to the sea. This is where the Sea Lord and his administration work to build the Second Fleet. The New City has impressive defences, while the streets and docks are patrolled by the Dietershafen Harbour Guard, a wellequipped regiment of halberdiers. The atmosphere in the New City is restrained — those expecting rowdiness and street fights are often surprised to see the mariners here are professional and disciplined. 

Looking down on Dietershafen is Manann’s Lantern, a temple to the Sea God that’s also a lighthouse. It is an important landmark — Dietershafen is notorious for the ‘Breath of Stromfels’, a thick sea fog which rolls into the town during the autumn. There is also a fraternity of blind pilots who can sail a ship into harbour from the feel of the sea alone, no matter the atmospheric conditions. 

There are many more temples to Manann reflecting his many aspects. The god plays a prominent role here, although Sigmar is more popular in Dietershafen than anywhere else on the Nordland coast. 

## **Manann’s Lantern**
The brazier atop Manann’s Lantern burns bright from sunset to sunrise or whenever the Breath of Stromfels shrouds the Eiger Bay. When a ship sights Manann’s Lantern on the shore, it is traditional to offer a prayer of thanks to the Sea God, for you never know when its light may save your life. 

The lighthouse tower is an ugly stone edifice, clearly built by Human hands less interested in aesthetics than function. During the Black Plague, Dietershafen was occupied by Skaven, who took the Lantern as their command post. Mandred ‘Skavenslayer’ won one of his first victories here, defeating the Clan Skryre engineer Sythar Doom and using his ‘Far-Claw’ invention to destroy a Skaven fleet at anchor in the harbour. Details of the antagonists have been lost to time, although Mandred’s triumph lives on with a statue of the Emperor mounted on the wall of the tower. 

Under the lighthouse tower is Dietershafen’s primary temple of Manann. The lower floors surround a vaulted chamber, lined with wooden slats like the inside of a ship turned upside down. High Priestess Lenge Flutbirger is a tough, passionate woman and a strong advocate for the Navy. She dismisses Salzenmund’s Wave Lord Otto Sider as a politician too focused on landlubbers. Her congregation are fighting mariners, working sailors, and the upper echelons of the Second Fleet. 

There are several priests subservient to High Priestess Flutbirger who spend most of their time at sea. Brother Wechster is assigned to the Imperial Navy and takes a particular interest in investigating spies and saboteurs along the coast. 

## The Oyster Feast
Each Brauzeit, the temple hosts the Oyster Feast, when the whole town gorges itself on shellfish and thanks Manann for his bounty. One night, as the townsfolk are sleeping off the feast, many people have the same dream — a horde of bipedal oysters marching on Manann’s Lantern for revenge. 

## Boons of Manann’s Lantern
The light from Manann’s Lantern reaches as far as the light from other lighthouses (see page 108). However, through a quirk of optics, or Manann’s beneficence, the light pierces mist and fog as if they were not there. Perception Tests made to spot the light are not modified by Visibility (see page 106). 

The Riddle Dock has a dry-dock, the first built in the Empire and sufficient for a ship under two hundred feet long. For a substantial price (10 GC per day), a ship can enter the dock for maintenance and repairs. The drydock belongs to Nielsine Bonde, a Dietershafen character famed for her brusque witticisms and intolerance for time-wasters. The dry-dock is an excavated cavity on the western edge of Riddle Dock. A ship sails in, the dock gates are closed and the water pumped out with a bucket dredge powered by donkeys. This exposes the keel and the hull below the waterline for repairs. Scraping Fouling from boats (see page 105) is a matter of routine here and is performed at half the normal price. 

## **The Behemoth Tavern**
Sailors looking to spend their hard-earned coin carousing will find the Behemoth Tavern disappointing. Its sign is a carved whale with a single horn, hanging in a steep narrow alley in the New City. The ceiling is low, the room sparsely lit with candles, and the conversation is earnest. Late in the night, patrons in their cups may break into song, but these are doleful chanties lamenting those lost at sea rather than ribald sailor’s tunes. 

The Behemoth’s clientele take their calling seriously, whether they be naval or mercantile crew on shore leave. They meet to discuss matters nautical and share yarns to keep them safe when they return to sea, an event heralded by their ship’s bosun coming into the tavern to fetch his crew back on board. A party visiting the tavern can make acquaintance with ships’ crews and captains, maybe finding a mentor to teach them sailing. 

In the south-west corner of Riddle Dock is a workshop where a soft-spoken old woman carves exquisite figureheads. Klara Beyer unconsciously uses latent magical ability to imbue her carvings with subtle enchantments. Characters with Second Sight detect faint eddies of Ghyran around her hands if they see her at work. A figurehead can be bought from Beyer at the usual price (see page 98). In addition to the normal effects, the figure has a 20% chance of carrying a minor enchantment — conferring a level of the _Luck_ Talent to the ship’s skipper whenever they’re on board. 

The Behemoth is the unofficial barrack room of the Sea Devils, a coastal regiment in the State Army of Nordland sponsored by the Köhlers. Unbeknownst to the authorities, Captain Siegfried Schmidt drinks here and surreptitiously recruits for his Renegades, a squadron of Ironfists he stole from the Navy. 

## We Got a Bite
## Schmidt’s Dilemma
When the Wolfship _Bold Otto_ goes into dry-dock, the shipwrights make a strange discovery. A cluster of Human, Orc, and Beastmen skulls have bitten into the keel and become stuck. When the _Otto_ sailed around Wrecker’s Point, the crew were troubled by green luminescence below the waves — and several ships have gone down there recently. 

Captain Schmidt enjoys socialising and recruiting right under the nose of the Imperial Sea Lord. Or he did enjoy it… until a lackey of the Smuggler Queen threatened to reveal his whereabouts. If he and his Renegades don’t start running contraband to the coast, she’ll turn him in. 

## **The Riddle Dock**
At the eastern edge of the Dietershafen seafront is an enclosed dockyard surrounded by maritime workshops and artisans’ premises. After passing through the entrance between stone quays, there is room enough for several seagoing vessels to moor by the jetties. 

The dock takes its name from an old Dietershafen ballad. In the song, a shipwright courts a mermaid who promises to marry him if he can answer a riddle. The shipwright can’t answer a riddle asked in the language of fish, so he dies of heartache and the mermaid is eaten by a kraken. The unfortunate pair are commemorated on a painted sign above the dock’s roadside entrance. 

## **Neues Emskrank**
## **The Ships’ Graveyard**
Amongst the dunes outside Dietershafen is a sandy hollow filled with wrecks to commemorate those lost at sea. It’s a maze of broken hulls and masts leaning at crazy angles, with a beached Wargalley at the centre. When a Dietershafen sailor is lost at sea, the bereaved family carve their name into some part of this ship — the woodwork is now inscribed with many thousands of names. 

At the mouth of the River Salz skulks the miserable town of Neues Emskrank — the legacy of a disastrous mercantile enterprise, shunned and avoided by most sensible travellers. 

Neues Emskrank is a town in permanent decline. In 2455 IC, Jens-Pieter Riemanns approached the Elector Counts and Empire merchants with a scheme to counter Marienburg’s domination of trade — build two new ports on the northern coast, Salkalten in Ostland and Neues Emskrank at the mouth of the Salz. Despite the fanfare when the ports opened in 2462 IC, the scheme was a disaster, made worse by surreptitious sabotage from Marienburg’s Directorate. 

The graveyard is haunted by Young Piet, a grisly spectre who floats through the wrecks at night, carrying his severed legs as his head flops loosely on his ruined neck. Piet’s family believe he was lost at sea, but he was actually murdered by Ostland sailors. 

Some officers swear that it is respectful to Manann to sail close to the Ships’ Graveyard and intone a mournful chanty. Most sailors find this a grim prospect and a sign that their skipper is ‘courting a haunting’. If such a task is performed, increase Manann’s Mood by 1 (see page 130), but reduce the Morale total to 0 (see page 124). 

The town today is a depressing place. Empty warehouses moulder in the rain, blank faces stare from broken windows, and weed-covered wrecks list in the empty wharves. Neues Emskrank squats on both banks of the Salz. The east bank was once the village Pugsblatter, taken over by Riemann’s Northern Mercantile Society. At the centre is Heringplatz, the original fish exchange and market square, where one finds the True Kipper, an inn filled with patrons who glower at strangers if they venture through the worm-ridden doors. Only lethargy keeps them from doing violence to outsiders. The old temple of Manann stands on the cliff top overlooking Drosselspule Bay. It is an ancient stone building, largely derelict since the new temple was built over the river. 

## That Went Well
Young Piet’s mangled corpse was dumped into a disused well in the Old City. His remains are still there, rotting in the stagnant water. If someone finds them, gives Piet a proper burial, and reveals his killers, he finds peace. 

The west bank of the Salz was built to a town plan, with rows of identical buildings and crumbling, grandiose architecture. It is a testament to the folly of those who invested in Neues Emskrank. Most residences are empty and streets remain half-built and overgrown. The new temple of Manann is the most impressive building, with three spires to evoke the Sea God’s trident. 

Those who visit Neues Emskrank try to leave soon after laying anchor. The locals are resentful of outsiders and sickly, something in the atmosphere of pessimism perhaps affecting them physically. There is meagre trade in Neues Emskrank — fish and some goods pass through the few intact wharves before travelling upriver. Illicit trade is common, especially through the old town. 

## City in the Mist
If one looks across Drosselspule Bay at dawn on a spring morning, the sunlight seems to carve strange patterns in the sea mist. Look for long enough and one can discern spires and soaring white towers in the bay, as if a lost city has risen from the depths. 

The people of Neues Emskrank insist this is the city once lost beneath the waves when its citizens wronged Manann. There are stories telling of fishermen lost to the city when it appears, after its fair citizens entice them in and take them from the mortal world forever. 

## **Fish Market**
The fish market in Heringplatz does a relatively brisk trade compared with the rest of the town. Fishermen drag their catch onto the docks each morning and sell them to traders in the fish market. The traders are notoriously sharp-tongued and opinionated. They shout their obnoxious views to one another over the hubbub of the market, berating customers and fishermen alike. The fish traders were vehement supporters of Nordland Separatism and still blame Middenheim and southerners for anything they dislike. 

The fish for sale in the market are varied, sold live and dead. Most are caught in Drosselspule Bay where shoals of fish proliferate. There are persistent rumours of a sunken city under the bay; lights are occasionally seen under the water, which heralds the influx of many fish. Superstitious folk won’t eat these as they believe they’re the souls of the drowned. Saltfish can be purchased here for rock bottom prices (see Maritime Trade on page 135). 

## **Leopoldschloss**
Leopoldschloss is the town’s main defence. Neues Emskrank may be a failure, but it is still a living town in a strategically important location, so the Nordland State Army maintain a presence here. The Leopoldschloss is a four storey keep surrounded by a perimeter wall which has seen better days, with impressive-looking inland defences and a lacklustre seaward face — a reflection of the Northern Mercantile Company’s skewed priorities. 

The permanent garrison is the Neues Emskrank company of the 1st Nordlander Handgunners (known as ‘Leopold’s Lions’). These men resent their posting — and not just because the miserable weather makes it difficult to keep blackpowder dry. Sergeant Horst Gustavson has taken to storing contraband on behalf of Nordland’s ‘Smuggler Queen’, with the help of his men. They share the profits equally, each fearing betrayal to their captain. 

A vessel that is short on crew may find it easy to pick up hirelings here — there are usually a few deserters looking for a quick way out of town. 

## Beneath the Weeds
The fishermen of Neues Emskrank bring strange things up in their nets. Broken masonry of exquisite quality, fine bones, and the occasional metal artefact. There is indeed a sunken settlement hidden by the thick weed of Drosselspule Bay. A scholar from Nuln speculates that the sunken city is the lost Asur city of Athel Toralien, but no High Elf will speak of the matter. She is in town asking around the fish market to find out more. 

## The Shell Game
Neues Emskrank is poorly defended and there is always a risk of Skaeling attacks. At dusk, red sails appear on the horizon and Leopold’s Lions make ready. As the the longships approach, the townsfolk bunker down in their homes. It’s a ruse — while everyone is distracted by the imminent ‘raid’, smugglers are landing a huge consignment of rum, gunpowder, and silk at the castle. 

## **Norden**
During the Age of Wars, Norse settlers founded a village they called Norden. The colonists adjusted to life in the south and became integrated into Imperial culture, trading goods from the sea with travellers on the MiddenheimErengrad road. 

Norden is now a middling town surrounded by mud flats, dunes, and quicksand, with a complex tracery of channels winding between shifting sandbanks and gravel shoals. Many years ago the port silted up and since then only shallow-drafted vessels can make landfall in Norden — and even then they require an experienced pilot or excellent charts to guide them into harbour. Commerce was reduced to fish, small cargoes, and a limited trade in amber, which is cast up by the sea onto beaches close to the town. 

Several months ago, Norden changed. Strangers are turned back at sea by a squadron of Wargalleys patrolling the waters near the town. State troops guard the roads and direct merchants to a new trading post in nearby Salzmorast. 

Those who do get into town find the place relatively innocuous, but they can’t reach the old port and feel watched — every beggar, shopkeeper, and urchin seems unreasonably interested in their presence. 

Norden has a secret. While the eyes of foreign powers are on Dietershafen and the shipbuilders expanding the Second Fleet, the powers-that-be are quietly building a new deep-water harbour at Norden. Hidden behind the maze of sandbanks, new channels to the sea are being dredged while the old port is refitted for Greatships and other vessels suited to crossing the Great Ocean. This is a clandestine attempt to build a new base from which the Empire can seize the riches of Lustria and the Southlands, circumventing the dominance of Marienburg over other maritime nations. 

Parties working for Gausser, Altdorf, or the Navy can enter the town with a letter of introduction. By sea, they need to anchor some distance offshore and take smaller boats into port. Those without permission need to travel on foot and keep their wits about them, for while they aren’t expressly forbidden from exploring Norden, they will be under surveillance and encouraged to leave by most townsfolk. 

## **Sea of Claws the Southern Coast**
## **Schloss Neurath**
The former seat of the Neurath family is a small castle just to the east of the town, situated in extensive grounds at the sea’s edge. The absentee noble family have turned it over to naval research under the auspices of Admiral Luther Hakluyt, who wants to bring the Empire’s navy kicking and screaming into the 26th century. A small cadre of Imperial engineers are billeted here, with access to workshops and labourers to help them develop new technologies for exploration and naval combat. 

Herr Wolfgang Kugelschreiber of Nuln has been coerced into developing submersible vessels using stolen Dwarf technology. The alchemist Sigismund the Mad is also here, trying to top the Hellhammer for insane innovation. Other projects include new alloys for armouring ships, improved swivel guns, and strange blends of tar which confuse the eye when painted onto a hull. The work here is not shared with the First Fleet command. 

In the right circumstances, Characters could obtain experimental technology for their ship or pick up a talented naval engineer who can make improvements to their vessel at sea. 

## Can I Leave?
People are looking for the missing engineers, and some of them would like a little more freedom than the Sea Lord or admiral allow them. When a dishevelled engineer flags down the Characters’ wagon on the road, he asks to be taken away from Norden, but won’t say why. Soon after, a patrol of roadwardens and sailors arrive looking for him. 

## An Honourable Gentleman
Captain Ralf Gottschalk is an affable infantry captain from Reikland, recovering in the Flint Harpoon tavern in Kriedeklippe for his health. He spends his time walking the cliffs and relaxing in the inn, talking with fishermen and others. He stands his rounds and locals think he’s a good soldier with none of the ‘airs and graces’ they expect from a captain and a Reiklander. In reality, Ralf is a Marienburger spy, trying to learn more about what’s happening in Norden. He has a small magical device: a glass eye which transmits what it sees up to ten miles in range. He’d really like to sneak it into Schloss Neurath. 

## **’ Sleeper S Mount**
Half a mile north of Norden is a rounded stone outcrop projecting from the sea. Hundreds of seabirds nest on its weathered face, and its surface is spattered with guano and the remains of gutted fish. Razorbills nest here (see **Imperial Zoo** page 77), so approaching too close is dangerous. Mermaids have been seen swimming around the rock. 

There is a tale of Manann fighting a sea daemon called Bloodwrack which he chained in a hollow under the rock. Should anyone land on Sleeper’s Mount, the legend claims they will be spirited inside to join a regiment of sleeping knights, who slumber around the trapped daemon, ready to restrain it should it escape its chains. 

## A Drunken Sailor
After too many ales, a sailor starts yarning about Sleeper’s Mount. He says there are figures moving about on the rock at night — cowled folk like monks walking in circles and even several mounted men… but there’s no way to transport a horse out there. The sailor thinks Manann has roused the sleepers, but there may be other explanations: smugglers, wreckers, or cultists.
